analysis.one_liner: Expands Affordable Care Act tax credits to families above 400% of the poverty line and lowers premiums.
analysis.headline: A bill to expand ACA premium tax credits to middle- and higher-income households got no committee vote before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would lift the income cap that today keeps households above 400% of the federal poverty line from getting any premium tax credit for coverage bought on the ACA marketplaces, and it would set the government's share on a sliding scale so no one pays more than 8.5% of income in premiums. It locks in and extends the richer subsidy schedule that Congress passed temporarily in 2021, starting with tax years after December 31, 2025. It never left committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Uninsured and underinsured households earning above 400% of poverty (roughly $62,000+ for a family of four) would become eligible for subsidies for the first time, and households just under the cap would see their premium share drop, under the sliding scale the bill writes into the tax code.

how_it_helps.text: Deletes the 'does not exceed 400 percent' limit in the ACA credit, making households above that income level eligible for premium tax credits for marketplace coverage.
Sets a sliding 'applicable percentage' table so households' premium share rises gradually with income and never exceeds 8.5% of income, replacing the current cliff at 400% of poverty.
Strikes the affordability-conforming provisions tied to the old income cap, so the expanded credit works cleanly with the rest of the tax code.
The changes apply to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025, so the enhanced, uncapped credit schedule would continue past the scheduled expiration of the temporary enhanced credits.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, since the expanded credits are refundable and the bill contains no offsets; the Treasury pays out more per policyholder as more people qualify and as the government's share of premiums rises. The subsidy dollars also flow through private health insurers, whose marketplace enrollment would grow.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers; insurers gain the enrollment

drawbacks.text: The bill has no funding offsets: expanding eligibility and raising the subsidy schedule is a direct federal cost, and the bill text contains no revenue provisions to pay for it.
The subsidies route through private marketplace insurers rather than a public option, so expanded federal spending also entrenches insurers' role as the channel for coverage.

Supporters of the 400% cap argue unlimited eligibility for higher-income households, where the credit reduces to a flat 8.5% share, benefits people who can afford coverage without help and adds to the deficit.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core benefit is real and targeted at a genuine problem: the 400% 'subsidy cliff' leaves families earning slightly above the cutoff facing full marketplace prices, sometimes thousands of dollars, and the bill removes it. The cost is a larger federal deficit with no pay-fors, and some of the money goes to relatively higher-income households. The design choice to keep subsidies inside private insurance is the honest trade: coverage expands, but the insurer role is locked in.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the House Ways and Means Committee, then to its Health subcommittee, and died there when the Congress ended without a markup or floor vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Lauren Underwood (D-IL) introduced the Health Care Affordability Act of 2024 in the House on September 24, 2024.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which holds jurisdiction over the tax code provisions it amends.
On December 17, 2024, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Health; no markup, vote, or floor action followed for the rest of the Congress.
The bill ended the 118th Congress on January 3, 2025 with no further action, leaving its provisions un-enacted.
Its sole action beyond referral was the subcommittee referral, meaning Ways and Means leadership never scheduled the bill for consideration.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Households above the subsidy cliff and families paying high marketplace premiums gained nothing because the bill died; the status quo of the 400% cap and the scheduled expiration of enhanced subsidies stands, which spares the Treasury the cost but leaves middle-income families with full marketplace prices and preserves insurers' existing risk pool rather than expanding it.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one; the subsidy cliff stayed

for.name: Rep. Lauren Underwood
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on September 24, 2024 to expand ACA premium tax credit eligibility and cap premium shares.

for.name: 35 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction; no House Republicans cosponsored it.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee leadership
against.role: Committee of referral under Chair Jason Smith
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral: no markup, no vote, no floor scheduling before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 35 cosponsors, plus the sponsor, were House Democrats; no Republicans signed on, and the Republican-controlled committee took no action.

industries.note: The bill would expand the insured marketplace by routing new subsidies to additional middle- and higher-income customers through private marketplace plans, growing insurers' enrollment and revenue while imposing no new rules on them. Coverage expands for families, but the private-insurance channel is locked in as the permanent vehicle for federal health support.

Refundable premium credits would be paid to more households with no offsets in the bill, a direct federal outlay. For families buying coverage the outlay is the benefit; for taxpayers generally it is added deficit spending.
